searchDocs.title: Introduction
searchDocs.content: Introduction Welcome to Openexus! Openexus is as unified platform for building Modules and Applications with simplicity and ease. With just a few clicks or some simple AI description, the application of your dreams is ready to be explored and shared. The only thing it takes is imagination. Today, digital creations are made up of monolithic applications with thousands of lines code; hunderdeds of thousands of lines of code even. We believe that with a well designed building blocks concept we can design a world where creations are simple to build using with highly reusable blocks. These blocks can span multiple languages and frameworks and remove all the complex and esorteric programming concepts that get in the way. Tutorial​ If you have not yet tried it out, it might be beneficial for you to walk through the Openexus Tutorial once. Playgrounds​ To get a sense of using Modules and connecting them together, try out the Openexus Playground.If you is more interested in developing a Module, our Openexus Developer Playground is a good place to start. Here you can build out a custom Module and populate it however you want.That said, if you are more serious about your work, why not get started by creating an Openexus Account where you can create custom Modules and Applications and have them saved and persistent across device and sessions. We are currently waitlisting users but you can Join the Waitlist and hope we invite you soon. The Open Module Specification​ The core aspect of Openexus is the Module. A Module is functionally just a building block of some aspect of a software system. By creating and combining Modules together, either your own or those of others, we can build larger and more complex systems. Think of Open Module as a smart Lego block for digital creations. Just like Legos... Modules can snap (aka connect) with other Modules.Each Module can have different features (different properties).Connecting multiple Modules together will form a more complex and interesting creation. At the heart of a Module, is what we call the Open Module Specification. Features​ The Open Module Specification is designed with these principles in mind: Simple to use by non-codersProgramming language agnosticBuilt to be highly reusableDesigned to be understood by AI Core Concepts​ There are a few Core Concepts one should know to get going with Openexus. These are ModulesInstancesPropertiesConnections We describe each of these below. Modules​ The primary building block of Openexus is the Module. A module is a building block (like Lego blocks) that allow users to piece them together to create interactive pages or applications. A Module can be as simple as a single function (e.g. age calculator) or as complex as an entire entity with complex visual and interactive elements (e.g. a map component). More fundamentally though, a Module is the description of a building block, the blueprint of it. It describes the module itself (the Manifest), the means of communication with the Module (the Properties), and the logic that is performed when the module is used or changes in some way (the Logic). We will go more into each of these concept in a minute. Instances​ An Instance is a running copy of a Module. If a Module is blueprint, an instance is a single implementation of that blueprint. If you think of a Module as a blueprint of a house, an Instance is the actual built house, a single stamped output of taking a blueprint and implementing against it. When you add a Module to an Openexus application, you are creating an Instance of that Module. Changes you make to that Instance are only applicable for that Instance and do not change the module itself. It is an important distinction to understand, the difference between a Module and an Instance. Properties​ Each module defines zero or more Properties. A Property is a single named data point of a Module. These data points each hold a specific value. The type of the value and what its is is entirely dependent on the Module being used. Connections​ Instances are tied to one another by a Connection. A Connection represents a binding between two specific Properties in two separate modules. You connect a Property on some Module to a Property on a different Module. When a Property changes on the first Module, the Property on the second Module is changed as well. We describe this as the Properties being "in-sync" meaning that what happens to one is reflected in the other.

searchDocs.title: Frameworks Overview
searchDocs.content: Frameworks Overview Openexus support for JavaScript/TypeScript allows for the optional usage of several popular open-source JavaScript/TypeScript frameworks. You may choose which framework to use from the list of supported frameworks below. Some Modules do not even need a Framework at all. A Module only needs a Framework if it has some sort of visual output. Even if a Module has visual output, using a framework is entirely up to you. It should also be noted that Openexus supports ANY framework you might want to work with, so long as we support the underlying programming languages. We provided a number of helpers and documentation for the most common frameworks, but any framework that renders to the DOM and HTML is perfectly fine with us. The Framework you choose will dictate the way your module is setup. Please see the Frameworks section documentation for more details. While using a framework may be helpful for some, it is entirely optional as Openexus supports standard Javascript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and DOM manipulation. For JavaScript and Typsescript modules, Openexus suports the following frameworks: Standard/Vanilla JS: DocumentationSolid: DocumentationReact: DocumentationVue: DocumentationSvelte: Documentation

searchDocs.title: Development Basics
searchDocs.content: Development Basics Each Module is essentially a building block with properties that can communicate with other Modules. To specify a Module, you then have to provide three (3) main pieces of information: Manifest: The general information about the Module, e.g. name, descriptionProperties: The list of properties that the Module haveCode: Some sort of logic/code that will run Code Language​ The openexus specification is designed to be language agnostic. Each module is a "black box" where the internal logic should not matter. The openexus.com platform supports a variety of languages such as Javascript, Typescript, and Python, and new languages are added often. Counter Example​ This is a basic Module with a button that will increment a ((value)) property every time the button is clicked. manifest.yaml name: Counter description: Simple counter example. properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view count: datatype: number default: 1 src/main.jsx function increment() { // Increment the value of ((count)) context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); } function render() { // Function that returns JSX can bind to // property of datatype `html` return ( <button on:click={increment}> Increment {context.get('count')} </button> ) } // Bind a function that returns JSX context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: Characters Count
searchDocs.content: Characters Count A simple Module that counts the number of occurrences of a character in string. This Module has no UI elements. Features used in this example: Read and write values to properties using context.get() and context.set().Subscribe to changes on specific properties. NOTE: This example does not include a UI/View and thus does not demonstrate those techniques nor framework usage. Example​ manifest.yaml name: Characters Occurance description: Count the occurrence of a character in certain text. icon: mdi:counter compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow properties.yaml string: datatype: text io: input required: true character: datatype: text io: input required: true count: description: The number of occurrence of a character in string. datatype: number io: output src/main.jsx let char = context.get('character'); let str = context.get('string'); function countCharacters() { let num = 0; let pos = str.indexOf(char); while (pos > -1) { pos = str.indexOf(char, pos + 1); num++; } context.set('count', num); } context.subscribe('string', (v) => { str = v; countCharacters(); }); context.subscribe('character', (v) => { char = v; countCharacters(); });

As such, creating modules in Openexus is mostly programming language and framework agnostic. However, Openexus cannot support every language or every frameworks, so please review our documnetation for usage and compatability. JavaScript and TypeScript are both fully supported by Openexus, including a complete API, a variety of popular frameworks, and suppport for external packages from NPM. searchDocs.title: React
searchDocs.content: React Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the React framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of React, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus React Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The React Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using React, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use React and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript React Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Setup the Helper SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use React and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within React, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as reactDom from 'react-dom/client'; import react from 'react'; import { setup } from 'openexus/react'; Setup the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx setup(context, react, reactDom); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base React component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/main.jsx // Create a render function function SomeComponent() { return ( <p>Hello world!</p> ); } // Set the UI property to the Component. context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent)); // alt Example​ Framework Specifics​ Using the React framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular React, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property must be obtained from Openexus. The Helper SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates a useable reactive signal from it. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => [getter, setter] Usage: const [count, setCount] = context.use('count'); Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the React library without using the Openexus React Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus React Helper SDK, one must manually createRoot and render on the element when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.tsx import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'; import ReactComponent from './ReactComponent.jsx'; context.set('ui', (el) => createRoot(el).render(ReactComponent())); Property References​ Without using the Openexus React Helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/ReactComponent.tsx import { useState, useRef, useEffect, createElement } from 'react'; function ReactComponent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(context.get('count')); useEffect(() => { context.subscribe('count', (v) => { setCount(v); }); }, []); useEffect(() => { context.set('count', count) }, [count]); return ( <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)} class='bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' > {`Count is ${count}`} </button> ); }

searchDocs.title: Writing Your First Module
searchDocs.content: Writing Your First Module To write your first Module, you will need to populate three things: A Manifest DeclarationAn optional Properties DeclarationOptional Code Manifest Declaration​ The Manifest Declaration describes your Module from a high level point of view. Things like name, description, categories, and documentation all go in your Manifest. The values you enter here help guide other in finding and using your Module, so they are very important. For your first Module, let us keep this very simple: We will enter just a name and a description. manifest.yaml name: My First Module description: This is my very first module and I am super excited to see it work! Properties Declaration​ A Properties Declaration describes specific data properties that a Module exposes. A property is holder of some value that a module uses for input, output, or both. Some properties in a Module are internal and just for a Module to use. Others are external and intended for other Modules that interact with the Module to use. The Properties Declaration is where one describes these properties. The Properties Declaration is made up of zero or more Property declarations. Each Property one wants to expose is described here. For each Property one must specify at most a Property Key, but we also recommend you also provide a datatype. The Property Key is the name of the Property one will use to reference that Property whenever we want to interact with it. It is strongly encouraged to use meaningful names that one can understand and that others will understand. Calling a Property a is not as helpful as calling is firstname. There are specific rules about what a Property Key must look like, so make sure to read Property Keys section of the Openexus Module Specification. properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view count: datatype: number default: 1! Code​ The Code of a Module defines the logic of what happens when the Module is executed and when some property the module is observing changes in some manner. Every Module executes its code when it is created each time and that code may also specify additional functions to execute as the Module changes. The details of this are up to the developer. The programming language and any framework a Module uses is flexible so long as Openexus supports it. For our first Module here, let us use JavaScript with the Solid framework. src/main.jsx import * as solidWeb from 'solid-js/web'; import * as solid from 'solid-js'; import { setup } from 'openexus/solid'; // Setup the context for use with solid setup(context, solid, solidWeb); function MyFirstSolidComponent() { // Creates a solid signal that is synced with the module property 'count' const [count, setCount] = context.use('count'); function increment() { // update the module property setCount(count() + 1); } return ( <div> <p>You have clicked the button {count()} times.</p> <button onClick={increment} class='mt-2 bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' > Click Me! </button> </div> ); } // Wrap MyFirstSolidComponent with render helper and set as ui context.set('ui', context.render(MyFirstSolidComponent)); Our First Module​

searchDocs.title: The Context Object
searchDocs.content: The Context Object Before we talk about the Context Object, a quick review of what Modules and Instances are is in order. A Module is the definition and all the bits necessary for the Module to be executed. An instance is a single execution of a Module. For example, if one has an Input Module and ran it two separate times, they would have two separate Instances, one for each execution. When we are writing a Module, the context object that we often work with, is the running instance. So in our prior example of two Input Instances, each has its own context. Using the ContextObject​ The Context Object is available in your code as the context variable. All of the members and methods described below are executed from the context object. For example, if we wanted to get a property value of the currently executing instance we would do so by calling `context.get(). ContextObject Members​ ContextObject Methods​ use(...args: unknown[]) => unknown Used for frameworks to obtain a reactive pass through to instance properties. For example., if you are working with a framework like React, you might use it to get a getter/setter for a property. The getter/setter is a react store and behaves as expected of a react store. trigger(propertyKey: string, event: unknown) => void Used to fire a Trigger event for the given propertyKey. The event object passed to this function will be provided as the event argument to down-stream trigger receivers. run(propertyKey: string, ...args: unknown[]) => void Used to execute an Action for the given propertyKey. Any additional arguments passed to the run function will be passed to the Action execution. get(propertyKey: string) => unknown Returns the current value of the given propertyKey. set(propertyKey: string, value: unknown) => void Sets the current value of the given propertyKey to value. Subscriptions, effects, and related signals bound to propertyKey will trigger after this value is updated. update(propertyKey: string, updateFunction: Function) => void Updates the current value of the given propertyKeys based on the return result of the updateFunction function. The updateFunction function has the following signature: <updateFunction> = (oldValue) => newValue mutate(propertyKey: string, mutator: Function) => void Updates the current value of the given propertyKeys based on the return result of the mutateFunction function. The mutateFunction function has the following signature: <mutateFunction> = (oldValue) => newValue subscribe(propertyKey: string | string[], handler: Function) => void Subscribe to notification when the given propertyKey (or propertyKeys) is changed. The handler is executed any time the propertyKey (or set of propertyKeys) changes. The handler function has the following signature: An alternate version of subscribe is allowed where one provides * as the property key, in which case all properties are subscribed. <handler function> = (newValue: unknown, oldValue: unknown, propertyKey: string) => void unsubscribe(propertyKey: string | string[], handler?: Function) => void Unsubscribe from notification when a property changes. One may specify a specific propertyKey or an array of propertyKeys to unsubscribe from. Unsubscribe will only occur on notifications that specifically match the given handler. Because functions are passed by reference in JavaScript/TypseScript this must be a referential match and not a content match. An alternate version of unsubscribe is allowed where one provides * as the property key, in which case all subscriptions that match the given handler function will be unsubscribed. notify(state:string, reason: string) => void Used to visually notify an instance that it is in a given state for a given reason. The possible state values are given below. If an invalid state is given, the notification WILL NOT be displayed. Possible states are: errorwarningsuccessinfofetchingfetchedloadingloaded context.render(renderFn: () => HTMLElement) => (el: HTMLElement) => void Used with modules that have to render some output. context.render() takes as its sole argument a function that when called returns a HTMLElement object. This HTMLElement is then appended DOM as the output of the module.

searchDocs.title: Vue
searchDocs.content: Vue Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the Vue framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of Vue, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus Vue Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The Vue Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Vue, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use Vue and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Vue Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Setup the Helper SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use Vue and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within Vue, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as vue from 'vue'; import { setup } from 'openexus/vue'; Setup the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx context = setup(context, vue); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base Vue component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/SomeComponent.vue <template> <p> Hello world! </p> </template> src/main.jsx // Set the UI property to the Component. import SomeComponent from './SomeComponent.vue'; context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent));`, Example​ Framework Specifics​ Using the Vue framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular Vue, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property reference must be obtained from Openexus. The SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates an reference to that object which can be interacted with to get and set the value. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => vueReference Usage: const countRef = context.use('count'); const foo = countRef.value; // getter countRef.value = 123; // setter Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the Vue library without using the Openexus React Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus Vue helper SDK, one must manually createApp and mount on the element when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.ts import { createApp } from 'vue'; import VueComponent from './VueComponent.vue'; context.set('ui', (el) => createApp(VueComponent).mount(el)); Property References​ Without using the Openexus Vue helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/helper.ts import { ref, watch, onUnmounted } from 'vue'; function usePropertyRef(propertyName) { const propertyRef = ref(context.get(propertyName)); let isInternalUpdate = false; // Watch for local changes and update the context const stopWatch = watch(propertyRef, (newValue) => { if (!isInternalUpdate) { isInternalUpdate = true; context.set(propertyName, newValue); isInternalUpdate = false; } }); // Subscribe to external changes const unsubscribe = context.subscribe(propertyName, (newValue) => { if (!isInternalUpdate) { isInternalUpdate = true; propertyRef.value = newValue; isInternalUpdate = false; } }); // Cleanup onUnmounted(() => { stopWatch(); unsubscribe(); }); return propertyRef; } src/VueComponent.vue <script setup> import { usePropertyRef } from './helper.ts'; const count = usePropertyRef('count'); // returns a ref function onClick() { count.value = Math.random(); } </script> <template> <button @click="onClick">Count: {{ count }}</button> </template>

Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as solidWeb from 'solid-js/web'; import * as solid from 'solid-js'; import { setup } from 'openexus/solid'; Setup the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx setup(context, solid, solidWeb); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base Solid component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/main.jsx // Create a render function function SomeComponent() { return ( <p>Hello world!</p> ); } // Set the UI property to the Component. context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent)); // alt Example​ In order to do this Openexus requires the usage of the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Solid SDK. The SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Solid, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. Framework Specifics​ Using the Solid framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular Solid, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property must be obtained from Openexus. The SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates a useable reactive signal from it. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => [getter, setter] Usage: const [count, setCount] = context.use('count'); Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the Solid library without using the Openexus Solid Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus Solid Helper SDK, one must manually createRoot and render on the element when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.ts import { render } from "solid-js/web" import SolidComponent from './SolidComponent.jsx'; context.set('ui', (el) => render(SolidComponent, el)); Property References​ Without using the Openexus Solid Helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/SolidComponent.tsx import { useState, useRef, useEffect, createElement } from 'react'; function SolidComponent() { const [count, setCount] = createSignal(context.get('count')); onMount(() => { context.subscribe('count', (v) => { setCount(v); }); }); createEffect(() => { context.set('count', count()) }) return ( <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)} class='bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' > {`Count is ${count()}`} </button> ); }

searchDocs.content: Svelte Openexus JavaScript/TypeScript support provides the ability to use the Svelte framework within a module. This provides the module with all the power of Svelte, JSX/TSX, and Reactive programming. In Openexus this may be achieved in one of two ways: via the Openexus Svelte Helper,or, Manually Do it Yourself. Openexus Helper SDK​ The Svelte Helper SDK provides a means to tell Openexus that you are using Svelte, and a way to interact with Openexus items such as modules and properties. To use Svelte and the Openexus Javascript/TypeScript Svelte Helper SDK... Import Framework and the SDK;Setup the Helper SDK;Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use Svelte and Openexus together. There may be additional things to do to work with Openexus items within Svelte, so make sure to read the Framework Specific Documentation below. Import Framework and the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx import * as svelteStore from 'svelte/store'; import * as svelte from 'svelte'; import { setup } from 'openexus/svelte'; Setup the Helper SDK​ src/main.jsx setup(context, svelte, svelteStore); Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what base Svelte component to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/SomeComponent.svelte <p> Hello world! </p> src/main.jsx // Set the UI property to the Component. import SomeComponent from './SomeComponent.svelte'; context.set('ui', context.render(SomeComponent));`, Example​ Framework Specifics​ Using the Svelte framework with Openexus has some small differences over regular Svelte, especially where one needs to interact with Openexus. These differences are outlined below. Property References​ In order to use a reference to a Openexus module property, the property must be obtained from Openexus. The SDK provides an easy to use way to do this with context.use(). context.use() takes the name of a specific module property (as defined in your properties.yaml file) and creates an object which allows setting the value and subscribing to changes on the value. Definition: context.use(<property-name>) => svelteSetter Usage: let count = undefined; // create our get value const setCount = context.use('count'); // get out setter from Openexus setCount.subscribe((value)=>count=value); // Setup a function to update our get value when the setter is invoked. Because of the manner in which Svelte makes getters just local variables, we need to create a local variable for count let count = undefined; and then we need to update it any time its associated setter is updated: setCount.subscribe((value)=>count=value);. The object returned by context.use() is called a svelteSetter. It has two functions: svelteSetter.set(value): Sets the value of this item.svelteSetter.subscribe(f): Executes the given function f whenever svelteObject.set() is called. Manual Setup​ For more specific control, one may choose to interface with the Svelte library without using the Openexus Svelte Helper SDK. Render UI​ Without using the Openexus Svelte Helper SDK, one must manually pass in the element through new SvelteComponent() when setting up the ((ui)) property. src/main.ts import SvelteComponent from './SvelteComponent.svelte'; context.set('ui', (el) => new SvelteComponent({ target: el })); Property References​ Without using the Openexus Svelte Helper SDK, one must manually create ref and setup subscription. This is an example helper function. src/SvelteComponent.vue <script> import { onMount } from 'svelte'; import { writable } from 'svelte/store'; const count = writable(context.get('count')); onMount(() => { context.subscribe('count', (v) => { count.set(v); }); }); count.subscribe((value) => { context.set('count', value) }) function onClick() { countWritable.set(count + 1); } </script> <button on:click={onClick} class='bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white py-2 px-4 rounded' >{`Count is ${count}`}</button>

searchDocs.title: Actions & Triggers
searchDocs.content: Actions & Triggers Actions and Triggers are the yin and yang of a Module, the push and pull of it. Actions are used to perform some behavior on a Module, to make it do something that the Module is capable of doing. Triggers are used to announce when a Module changes in a noteworthy way that in which other Modules would be interested. Together Actions and Triggers work together to announce changes and respond to those changes. Actions​ An Action is a Property with a datatype of action. Actions are code that run when activated. They can be activated manually, or by being connected to a Trigger. The code associated with an action is a function that is set as a value to that action, as shown here: properties.yaml someAction: datatype: action src./main.js context.set('someAction', ()=>{ ... code to be executed on action invocation ... }); Setup an action​ To bind a function to an action property, simply call context.set() as shown here: src./main.js context.set('someAction', ()=>{ ... code to be executed on action invocation ... }); Example​ In this example, the Generate Random action can be clicked on and then the Run Action button can be clicked. This will cause a new random number to be generated and set into the ((randomNumber)) property. Run an action​ One can programmatically execute an action using he context.run() method to execute an Action Property. Since we are developing the module, calling run may seem strange, but it is useful for testing and a few edge cases. main.js context.run('send_email'); Additionally, the concept of running an action makes more sense when you consider the need to execute an action on another instance's context, instead of the context of the module you are writing. main.js const instance = context.getInstance('9a3b8b8d-18e2-4951-a7cc-de8ff5dd42fd'); instance.run('send_sms'); Triggers​ A Trigger is a Property that is used to notify connected instances of some event. An event can be anything you want it to be. Events are typically due to some change in the Module like a mouse click or a photo taken. It depends on the Module and the use casebu t is entirely up to you when to use a trigger. Typically we call the execution of a Trigger a "firing". So we tend to say "fire a trigger" to describe this process. Triggers my be connected to Actions such that when the connected Trigger fires, the connected Action is run. Firing a Trigger​ To fire off a Trigger property, simply call the context.trigger() function as shown here... main.js context.trigger('some_trigger'); Example​ In this example, the defined trigger ((my_trigger)) is executed once every five seconds, causing a new random number to be set in the ((randomNumber)) property. main.js // listens for the trigger ((my_trigger)) to be triggered and updates ((randomRumber)) // with a new random number when it is. context.subscribe('my_trigger',() => { context.set('randomNumber', Math.round(Math.random() * 100)) }); // Fires the trigger every 5 seconds. setInterval(() => { context.trigger('my_trigger'); // Fire a trigger every 5 seconds }, 5000); `}

searchDocs.title: JavaScript/TypeScript SDK Overview
searchDocs.content: JavaScript/TypeScript SDK Overview Openexus provides a SDK that sits between Openexus and your code. The SDK provides access to modules, instances, properties, etc. Basically, everything in Openexus can be found via the SDK. Context​ The SDK is exposed as the context global variable in your code. You can use this context object for a variety of purposes such as adding an instance of a module, accessing properties on the module, getting notified when something changes in Openexus, or execute an action. src/main.js // read the value of a property context.get('foo'); // set the value of a property context.set('foo', 'bar'); // set foo === bar // get notified when something changes context.subscribe('foo', (value,key) => { ... do something magical ... }); etc... There's a lot of things you can do, so please read the documentation below to find out more about context and how to access specific things... More about... Manipulating PropertiesSubscribe to property changesWork with Actions & TriggersImport PackagesModule NotificationsRenderingWorking with Views and ViewportsThe Context ObjectJS/TS Openexus SDK Cheat Sheet

searchDocs.title: Notifications
searchDocs.content: Notifications Sometimes it is helpful to convey the state of a module such as progress, warnings, or errors. This is called Module Notification and it is very simple to do. The context.notify() function allows your to specify a notification state, and a notification message to display. context.notify() has the following signature: context.notify(<state>, <message>); Where state is one of the Notification State values shown below, and message is any string of text you want to display. Notification States​ The following notification states are supported: success - Indicates some successful action or operation.warning - Indicates the module is in a warning state and needs attention.error - Indicates the module is in an error state and failing to execute for some reason.info - Indicates some information to the module user.fetching - Indicates the module is fetching data from an external source. The fetching state is not automatically changed to the fetched state. It is incumbent on the developer to change to the notification states when the fetching operation is done.fetched - Indicates the module completed fetching data from an external source.loading - Indicates some portion of the module is in the loading state. The loading state is not automatically changed to the loaded state. It is incumbent on the developer to change to the notification states when the loading operation is done.loaded - Indicates the the module has loaded completely. NOTE: Internally Openexues does not use the module notification to indicate if a module is loaded or not. loading and loaded are provided purely for module developers to use. NOTE: Any other state value that is not described above will result in no notification shown. NOTE: The loading state and the fetching state are not automatically changed to the loaded state or fetched state automatically. It is incumbent on the developer to change to these notification states when the loading/fetching operation is done. Examples​ In this example the module will cycle through a series of loading states to show off the differernt styles. src/main.ts context.notify('error', 'Error occured!'); context.notify('warning', 'Authentication may be required'); context.notify('success', 'Success!'); context.notify('info', 'Parsing data'); context.notify('fetching', 'Downloading data...'); context.notify('fetched', 'Data downloaded!'); context.notify('loading', 'Calculating...'); context.notify('loaded', 'Done processing!'); Example​ In this example the module simulates fetching data from Github, showing a notification it is Fetching data... and then a notification of Data Fetched! when the data is returned and populated into ((Github_Issues)). The simulation will then reset itself after 10 seconds and then run again. src/main.ts setTimeout(() => { context.notify('fetching', 'Fetching data...'); const response = new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(() => resolve({'github': 'results'}), 3000); }) if (!response.ok) { response.then((result) => { context.set('githubIssues', result); context.notify('fetched', 'Data Fetched!'); }) } else { context.notify('error', 'Error Fetching Data.'); } }, 1000)

searchDocs.title: Vanilla / Standard / No Framework
searchDocs.content: Vanilla / Standard / No Framework One option for JavaScript/TypeScript development is to not use a framework at all and just relying on plain JavaScript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and DOM manipulation. To do so one must manually build out their DOM structure via JavaScript/TypeScript DOM calls and manually setup the details of the HTML. Setup and Usage​ NOTE: Because Vanilla JS/TS is not using a framework it requires less setup over other frameworks. To use Vanilla JS/TS... Setup a Renderer. Once the above steps are satisfied the module is ready to use react and Openexus together. Setup a Renderer​ A renderer tells a module what to display for the module. Some modules may not require a renderer, but most do. If you have a UI property, or a property that has a datatype of html you will need to setup a renderer for it as shown here. src/main.js // Create a render function function render() { // Your DOM setup and manipulation go here... } // Set the ((ui)) property to be the render function context.set('ui', context.render(render)) Example​

searchDocs.title: Imports
searchDocs.content: Imports A module may import a variety of both relative and external code or packages. Largely importing adheres to standard JavaScript/TypeScript rules, but there a few special edge cases one should be aware of depending upon the style of import and what is being imported. Standard Imports​ JavaScript/Typescript both support standard imports via their import keyword. These can be relative code (eg, ./MyOtherCode.js) or external packages (eg. express). Relative Imports​ A relative import refers to any file located within your module development space. A relative import always starts with either ./ or ../. Please note it is not possible to import something below the root of your project. For example, if given the following tree structure... ./ manifest.yaml properties.yaml src/ main.js module1/MyModule1.js module2/MyModule2.js The following imports would work: From src/main.js: import Module1 from './module1/MyModule1.js'; import Module2 from './module2/MyModule2.js'; from src/module1/MyModule1.js: import Module2 from '../module2/MyModule2.js'; from src/module2/MyModule2.js: import Module1 from '../module1/MyModule1.js'; External Imports​ Any NPM package can also be imported using the import JavaScript/TypeScript keyword. import chartjs from 'chartjs/auto'; When an import occurs, Openexus parses the module code and pulls any NPM package imports out, and loads them. Importing UMD Javascript/Typescript packages​
