searchDocs.title: Styling
searchDocs.content: Styling Openexus suports two different styling options when working in JavaScript/TypeScript: Tailwind and imported CSS/SCSS/SASS/LESS; whichever Styling library is preferred for module development. All Styling options work with all JavaScript/TypeScript supported JavaScript/TypeScript frameworks. Tailwind Styling​ Tailwind is supported out of the box. Most Tailwind classes are supported and enabled on all frameworks. For more information on tailwind, please visit: https://tailwindcss.com/ Tailwind Example​ <div class='p-4 bg-blue-200'>Hello World!</div> Imported CSS Styling​ One can also import a CSS file in the module file structure. In addition to supporting CSS, Openexus also support SCSS, SASS, and LESS CSS formatting. CSSSCSSSASSLESS src/styles.css button { font: 100% Helvetica, sans-serif; background: #ff9900; } src/main.js import "./styles.css"; function render(element) { const node = document.createElement('button'); node.innerHTML = 'Click me!'; element.appendChild(node); } context.set('view', render);

searchDocs.title: categories
searchDocs.content: categories The categories Manifest field is used to determine how to organize Modules when looking for a module in Openexus. A Module may specify up to two categories, a Primary category and a Secondary Category. Each categories is specified in the following form: <main category>/<subordinate category>[, <main category>/<subordinate category>] For example: manifest.yaml name: My Simple Module categories: input/text The following Main Categories are recommended: inputpresentationutility Within each of the Main Categories, the following Subordinate Categories may be used: input input/textinput/numberinput/selectinput/mediainput/buttoninput/colorinput/datetime presentation presentation/layoutpresentation/textpresentation/numberpresentation/mediapresentation/datetimepresentation/data utility utility/textutility/colorutility/number

searchDocs.title: Specification Overview
searchDocs.content: Specification Overview The Openexus Module Specification defines the structure and details to describe a Module and all of its supporting code and assets. When a Module is used, the Openexus Module Specification is interpretted to produce the Module and execute the code. There are three (3) major components to the specification: a Manifest declarationa Properties declarationSource Code Each of these components is described below and in the following sections. Manifest​ The manifest declaration describes the metadata of the Module and all additional configuration for it. This include the name of the Module, a description of it, an icon for it, and all supporting configuration. It should be noted, that the properties of a Module are described outside of this file, but everything else is configured within the manifest. A manifest is required for every Module. A very simple manifest may have these fields: manifest.yaml name: Number Doubler description: Simple module that doubles a number. icon: mdi:star compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow Read more information about the contents of manifest declaration. Properties​ The properties declaration describes the specific properties of a Module. A Module may have zero or more properties and each property is configured in this properties declaration. properties.yaml value: description: Provide the number to double. datatype: number default: 1 double: description: The doubled value. datatype: number default: 2 Read more information about the contents of properties declaration. Source Code​ The source code of a Module consists of zero or more source files in the programming language specified in the manifest. Source code is the code executed when a module starts and when any observed property changes. Source code is not required for all modules. Source code may have any structure desired, but it is strongly recommended that it be placed under a folder named /src. The default source code entry point is src/main.js and it is recommended that all code begins there. src/main.js context.subscribe('value', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); Read more information about the source code. Example​ In this example one may change the value of ((value)) and the value of ((double)) will be changed.

searchDocs.title: Code Configuration
searchDocs.content: Code Configuration The Source Code of a Module is any part of the Module's specification that contains executable software instructions in the form of a supported programming language. When a Module is used the source code is interpretted and run to produce the Module's output. Additionally, as the Module is interacted with, the source code can respond to the changes in the Module and produce different output. Some Modules require no source code while other require a little source and still others require lots of source code. It all depends on what the objective of the Module is. Supported Languages​ Currently Openexus supports the following languages for source code: JavaScriptTypeScriptPython (Coming Soon!) Frameworks​ In addition to supported languages, some languages also have specific frameworks that work with Openexus. For example, you can write your Module's Source Code in JavaScript using the React framework. This means that the Source Code supports the language and framework you are most comfortable using. Using a Framework is mostly only useful when creating a Module that has a UI component to it and takes advantage of these UI frameworks. Currently the following frameworks are supported within the following languages: JavaScript & TypeScript Vanilla (Standard JS/TS without framework)SolidReactVueSvelte Openexus SDK​ In order to interact and work within Openexus your Source Code will need to use the Openexus SDK. The SDK defines a series of Types, Objects, Functions, etc, as appropriate to the language of choice, that are used to manipulate the Module and its surrounding instances. The SDK is its own section of this documentation and further broken down by language of choice. Please visit the SDK sections below to learn more about all the SDK calls. JavaScript and TypeScript SDK Whenever possible Openexus has attempted to make the SDK as similar as possible across languages; however, this is not always entirely feasible and differences and nuances may exist between them.

searchDocs.title: direction
searchDocs.content: direction Properties by default are reactive and bi-directional, meaning they are both read and write. However, indicating how the Property is used can be very useful for the user to understand the intent of the properties. The direction Property field can be used to do this. If a Property is only read and never written (e.g. only context.get('query') and not context.set("query", newValue)), it would be an input property. If a Property is written (e.g. only context.get('result') and not context.set("result", newValue)), it would be an output property. If a Property is both read and written in a reactively way (e.g. both context.get('value') and context.set("value", newValue) are used in the module), the direction would be both. direction values​ both: This Property can be both read (get) or written (set).output: This Property can only be read (get).input: This Property can only be written (set). Example​ properties.yaml query: datatype: text direction: input result: datatype: json direction: output value: datatype: json direction: both

searchDocs.title: Subscriptions
searchDocs.content: Subscriptions It is often important to be made aware of when something changes in Openexus; notably, properties on a module as they change state. This is acheived through the SDK subscription system. Whenever something changes, everything that is subscribed to listen for changes gets notified. Single Subscription​ To listen to a property change, we simply use the context.subscribe() function. context.subscribe() has the signature context.subscribe(<property name>, <subscribe function>). Whenever <property name> changes, <subscribe function> is executed. The <subscribe function> receives the new values, the old value, and the property name as arguments: mySubscribeFunction(newValue, oldValue, propertyName). Here's an example: const sub = context.subscribe('count', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); One can also To stop listening to a property change, simply call unsubscribe() with the same arguments you called subscribe. Here's an example again: const sub = context.subscribe('count', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); setTimeout(() => { // Stop listening to ((count)) changes after 10s sub.unsubscribe('count', subFunc); }, 30000); src/main.ts const sub = context.subscribe('count', (value) => { // Set ((double)) when ((count)) changes context.set('double', value * 2); }); setTimeout(() => { // Stop listening to ((count)) changes after 30s sub.unsubscribe(); }, 30000); `} Multiple Subscriptions​ If you need to subscribe to mutliple properties at once, you can pass in an array of property names, instead of a single property name. If any property of the array changes, the <subscriber function> will be called for that property. If multiple properties change, the <subscribed function> will be called one time for each property changed. src/main.js const sub = context.subscribe(['count', 'count2'], (value) => { context.set('total', context.get('count') + context.get('count2')); }); Subscribe to all properties​ Sometimes it is useful to subscribe to all property for a given module at once. This can be accomplished using context.subscribeAll(). context.subscribeAll() has the following signature: context.subscribeAll(<subscriber function>). Whenever any property of the module changes, the subscription will be called. If multiple properties of the module change, a call for each changed properly will be run. src/main.js const sub = context.subscribeAll((value) => { context.set('total', context.get('count1') + context.get('count2') + context.get('count3')); }); Unsubscribing​ As mentioned above one can unsubscribe from a property by passing the same arguments to context.unsubscribe() that were used to make the subscription in the first place. However, it is worth nothing that when you pass an array of property names to context.subscribe() you may either unsubscribe to all of them by passing the same array of property names to context.unsubscribe(), or you may unsubscribe from a single one of the property names in the array at a time by calling context.unsubscribe() with a single property name.

searchDocs.title: Gallery
searchDocs.content: Gallery A gallery Module that renders connected UIs. Features used in this example: Example on how to use Viewports and the 'web-view[]' datatype. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid A gallery module that renders a connected UI without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Gallery description: A gallery module that renders connected UI. properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view slot: datatype: 'web-view[]' src/main.jsx import { For, Show } from "@modules-js/components"; // This render function simply renders each connected UI // in a staggered way function render() { return ( <Show when={context.getExtended('slot').length > 0} fallback={<div>No UIs connected to slot!</div>} > <div style={{ position: 'relative' }}> <For each={context.getExtended('slot')}> {(ui, index) => ( <> <div>{context.data?.()}</div> </> )} </For> </div> </Show> ); } // Bind a function that returns JSX context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: Manipulating Properties
searchDocs.content: Manipulating Properties Modules have properties to which one can read or write a value. It is the most common and basic task when developing a module. Fortunately, it is also incredibly easy. Read a Property Value​ The simpiliest way to read data from a property is to use context.get('<property_name>'). For example... properties.yaml count: datatype: number default: 1 main.js console.log('Count is', context.get('count')); output Count is 1 Changing a Property​ Writing values to a property is also fairly simple, but for more complex values may require a bit more. Primitive datatypes such as text, number, and boolean are easy. More complex datatype like arrays and object require a little more thought, although it depends largely on what is being accomplished. Writing a Value​ The recommended and simpiliest way to write a value to a property is to use context.set('{property_name}', {value}). This write operation will completely replace the prior value. For non-primitive values like arrays and object this may be less desireable; in those cases a mutate may be more appropriate. Additionally, some time you need to see the prior value as part of the change operation; in this case you can use the update context function instead of set. Here is an example of Writing a Value... main.js context.set('count', 2); // set value to a property output Count before write is 1 Count after write is 2 Update Values​ Optionally, if you need to reference the prior value as part of writing a value, it is better to use context.update(). context.update() has the form context.update(<property name>, <update function>). Here's an example: main.js context.update('count', (prev) => prev + 1); Update Object Values​ If you are working with objects, you can also do fine-grain updates using context.mutate. Fine-grain mutations are preferred in reactive systems because we can reactively update the other connected properties in a fine-grained manner; meaning we can only update the part that changed, as opposed to the whole object. context.mutate() has the form context.mutate(<property name>, <mutate function>). Here's an example usage: main.js context.mutate('obj', (obj) => { obj.list[0] = '123'; obj.list.push(456); });

searchDocs.title: Viewports
searchDocs.content: Viewports A Module can be used to render other Modules, usually providing a specific type of layout for those child Modules. This is accomplished by using a property called a viewport. A viewport is a specific property setup to connect with other Modules rendering. A viewport property looks like this: properties.yaml viewport: datatype: 'web-view[]' Because a viewport is rendering out other Modules View properties, we should probably also have a View property along with our viewport to display the output. Like this... properties.yaml view: datatype: web-view viewport: datatype: 'web-view[]' Once properties are setup, there remains but one thing to do: render viewport input to view output. The manner to do this is slightly different for each framework, but substantively its the same idea; render each View connected to the viewport in some order, applying some layout or otherwise as one goes. The best way to demonstrate this is to show one how to do it. VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid This is a very basic example to illustrate the concept of a viewport. Consider using a templating engine like pug, hyperscript, lit or a frontend framework. src/main.js function render(element) { // Since ((viewport)) has the datatype 'web-view[]', an array of render functions will be returned const viewport = context.get('viewport') || []; // Loop through each item and call the function provided viewport.forEach((viewRender) => { const viewElement = document.createElement('div'); element.appendChild(viewElement); // Pass in the element for the render function to mount viewRender?.(viewElement); }); } context.set('view', render);

searchDocs.title: Counter
searchDocs.content: Counter Render a button that when clicked, increments a value. Features used in this example: Reading and writing values to properties (context.get and context.set).Render UI elements using different frameworks. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid Simple counter button example without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Counter (JavaScript) description: An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. categories: starter/javascript,starter/vanilla keywords: starter,javascript,vanilla,counter icon: logos:javascript compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view count: datatype: number description: The number of times the button has been clicked since this application was started. This represents using a simple Property in the Openexus system. default: 1 src/main.js /** * An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple * button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. */ let button; // Define a render function to return our HTMLElement to display. function render() { // Create the element. button = document.createElement('button'); // Populate the element. button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; // Openexus components use tailwind by default, but you can define CSS // classes and styles in your preferred manner. button.classList.add('bg-blue-500', 'hover:bg-blue-700', 'text-white', 'py-2', 'px-4', 'rounded'); // For our button we want to mutate our count state when it is clicked. button.addEventListener('click', (value) => { context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); }); return button; } // Register to be notified when ((count)) changes. context.subscribe('count', (value) => { if (button) button.innerHTML = `Count is ${value}`; }); // Set our render function to the ((ui)) property for rendering. context.set('ui', context.render(render));

searchDocs.title: Quick Start
searchDocs.content: Quick Start Creating a Module​ Each Module is essentially a building block with Properties that can communicate with other Modules. A Module is a "black box" where the internal logic is completely hidden from another Module. Everything that a Module does, everything it allows other Modules to connect to, these things are entirely up to the Module author. To create a Module, we need these pieces of information: Manifest Declaration: The general information about the Module, e.g. name, description.Properties Declaration: The list of properties that the Module exposes.Code: Optional code or logic that will execute on behalf of the Module. While it is entirely possible to create a Module with only a Manifest, Properties make the Module usable by others, and Code makes the Module more powerful and useful. Code & Programming Languages & Frameworks​ The Openexus Module Specification is designed to be language agnostic. As such, the programming language a Module uses is up to the Module author. The openexus.com platform supports a variety of programming languages such as Javascript, Typescript, and Python, and new languages are added often. Additionally, a programming language often has multiple frameworks that allow easier and faster software development. These frameworks are entirely dependent on the programming language being used. That said, Openexus supports a variety of frameworks for different programming languages. Which framework, if any, a Module uses is entirely up to the Module author. For more information regarding support programming languages and frameworks, please see the Openexus Module Specification > Code section. An Example Module​ This is a basic Module with a button that will increment a ((value)) Property every time the button is clicked. VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid Simple counter button example without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Counter (JavaScript) description: An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. categories: starter/javascript,starter/vanilla keywords: starter,javascript,vanilla,counter icon: logos:javascript compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view count: datatype: number description: The number of times the button has been clicked since this application was started. This represents using a simple Property in the Openexus system. default: 1 src/main.js /** * An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple * button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. */ let button; // Define a render function to return our HTMLElement to display. function render() { // Create the element. button = document.createElement('button'); // Populate the element. button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; // Openexus components use tailwind by default, but you can define CSS // classes and styles in your preferred manner. button.classList.add('bg-blue-500', 'hover:bg-blue-700', 'text-white', 'py-2', 'px-4', 'rounded'); // For our button we want to mutate our count state when it is clicked. button.addEventListener('click', (value) => { context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); }); return button; } // Register to be notified when ((count)) changes. context.subscribe('count', (value) => { if (button) button.innerHTML = `Count is ${value}`; }); // Set our render function to the ((ui)) property for rendering. context.set('ui', context.render(render)); Beyond Getting Started​ By now, you know the basics of a module creation! Examples is a good place to see how to create various different types of modules.Specification is a good place to learn about the complete specification of a module.Javascript/Typescript is a good starting point to learn more about using the SDK to create modules.

searchDocs.title: Manifest Declaration
searchDocs.content: Manifest Declaration Each Module requires a Manifest declaration. In the Manifest declaration you define the Module configuration as described in the Manifest Fields below. A manifest must include, at a minimum, the name field and the compiler field, but may also include any of the optional fields like icon or keywords. The description field is technically optional, but strongly recommended. manifest.yaml name: Number Doubler description: Simple module that doubles a number. icon: mdi:star compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow Manifest Fields​ name - Visible title for the Module, displayed to whenever the design view of a Module is shownin Openexus. compiler - What compiler should be used for this module. The compiler setting signals to Openexus how to compile and execute the code, including what, if any, framework is to be supported. Currently the following values are allowed: vanilla, vue@3, react@19, svelte@5, solidjs@2. This is a required field, and if not provided will cause an error. vanilla - Standard TypeScript/JavaScript compiler with no extra framework.react@19 - Standard TypeScript/JavaScript compiler with support for the React frameworks, version 19.solid@2 - Standard TypeScript/JavaScript compiler with support for the Solid frameworks, version 2.svelte@5 - Standard TypeScript/JavaScript compiler with support for the Svelte frameworks, version 5.vue@3 - Standard TypeScript/JavaScript compiler with support for the Vue frameworks, version 3. description - A description about what the module does. The description of the Module should be relatively short. To add more details beyond the description, use the documentation field. icon - Openexus supports Iconify's icon sets and one can reference one of those exposed public icons to display for the module. For more information about Iconify, please see https://icon-sets.iconify.design. documentation - Longer form details about how the Module works and anything anyone using the Module would need to know or do. categories - Categorical tags for the Module used when organizaing Modules for user selection. You may specify up to two categories in a comma separated format from the following category list. Any category that does not meet this list or exceeds the category allowance will be ignored. Please see the Categories section below. keywords - Useful keywords that this Module may be found under when searching for new Modules. You may specify any number of keywords as a comma-separated string. Keywords are case-insensitive and may contain spaces, but may not start with or end with a space. thumbnail - A thumbnail image to represent this Module. A thumbnail must be a fully formed url to an image externally available. screenshots - Zero or more screenshots to illustrate this Module and how it works. Screenshots must be a fully formed url to an image externally available. environment - What execution environment in which this module runs. Currently supports browser, js-runtime, or browser|js-runtime. browser: Execution of this module is limited to browser-based environments.js-runtime: Execution of this module is limited to non-browser environments.browser|js-runtime: Execution of this module is allowed in either browser or js-runtime environments. sandbox - What sandboxing container should Openexus use. That is, how should Openexus contain the module code from leaking out into other modules and the underlying environment. The only value currently supported is browser.shadow. browser.shadow: The execution container for this module uses Browser ShadowRoot to constrain execution. dependencies - Used to specify a list of dependencies. Has the form of <library>@<version>. For example svelte/store@3.3.2 or chartsjs@12.4.2. Currently all dependencies listed here must be available on esm.sh. Please make sure the dependency and version desired is available there. Examples​ Some examples of manifest declarations. A Simple Input Field Example​ name: Input description: Input field for user input purpose: Input field to accept user input. Great for entering text, numbers, url, emails, etc. Useful to bind with other modules that require user input. instructions: icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow compiler: solid@2 dependencies: name: Button description: A simple button that can trigger actions icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow compiler: solid@2 dependencies: A Button Example​ name: API Fetch description: A simple button that can trigger actions purpose: Input field to accept user input. Great for entering text, numbers, url, emails, etc. Useful to bind with other modules that require user input. instructions: icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow compiler: react@19 dependencies: A Fetch Example​ name: Unit Conversion description: A conversion module that can convert between two values. Types of conversion includes time, length, data, volume, area, mass, temperature, power, angle, and more. icon: iconoir:input-field categories: input keywords: input screenshots: - https://example.com/screenshot.png - https://example.com/screenshot2.png environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow compiler: vue@3 dependencies: A Unit Conversion Example​

searchDocs.title: order
searchDocs.content: order Modules can have a lot of properties. The order Property field can be used to indicate the importance of the Property. Larger order numbers are more important and thus have better visibility. Negative numbers are automatically collapsed and initially hidden. The order number you set is a hint on where a Property should be displayed relative to the other properties. order value​ The order Property field takes a number. The number you give order determines how important the Property is when displayed. Higher positive numbers are displayed higher up and thus more visible.Lower positive numbers are displayed lower down and this less visible.zero is treated as a lower positive number.Negative numbers are collapsed in the display and hidden behind the "More..." toggle. NOTE: order is entirely about how properties are displayed and has no impact on the property itself. NOTE: If a property has a group then the order of properties within that group is what we are defining with the order property. Where a group is displayed is not impacted by order or properties with an order property. That is to say, if we have both group and order on a property, the order value is only relevant within the group and not within the greater hierarchy of properties. Example​ properties.yaml value: datatype: text order: 10 # Most prominent because it has the highest order min: datatype: number order: -1 # Collapsed by default because negative max: datatype: number order: -1 # Collapsed by default because negative label: datatype: text # Default order of 0

searchDocs.title: group
searchDocs.content: group Use the group Property field to group a Module's related properties together. When a Module is displayed to a user, grouped properties are called out into their own area which contains each Property of the group. The group value is purely for display purposes and has no impact on any other aspect of using a Property. group field​ The group Property field can contain any string you want, but it is desirable to keep this short (less than 16 characters or so) and minmize any non-alphanumeric characters. group ordering​ When a Module has groups the are renderer in the order they first occur within the Properties Declaration. For example, if we had the below properties with groups defined the order of the groups would be Visualization followed by Options. properties.yaml value: datatype: text show_value: datatype: boolean group: Visualization min: datatype: number group: Options max: datatype: number group: Options Example​ properties.yaml value: datatype: text min: datatype: number group: Options max: datatype: number group: Options show_value: datatype: boolean group: Options

searchDocs.title: Using Secrets
searchDocs.content: Using Secrets Openexus supports a special datatype called a secret. A property of type secret is functionally of type text but its contents cannot easily be revealed. This allows for the storage of unique secure data such as API Tokens and passwords in a secure manner that do not leak to outside users. Secret Storage​ Secrets are stored in the project or page settings of a Stitcher. Secrets that are used by multiple pages should be added to the Project Settings. Secrets used by only a single page should be stored in the Page Settings. In either case Secrets can be found under the RESOURCES section of these settings. To create a Secret one must provide two things: key - A unique (to the project or page) name for this secret. The Secret key is used wherever one needs to refer to the secret.value - The value represents the hidden secret itself. This is where one would store the API Token or Password that they want protected. Using Secrets​ When a instance has a property that has a value of secret one can select which secret key (from the Project Settings or Page Settings) they wish to associate with that property. The Secret is never displayed and cannot be connected to a non-secret property. However, when that secret is used, the secret selected is swapped for its secret value and that is used instead.

searchDocs.title: Chart
searchDocs.content: Chart A chart Module that imports ChartJS and uses it to render a nice bar chart. Features used in this example: NPM imports.UI rendering using various frameworks. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid A chart module without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: ChartJS description: Chart powered by ChartJS! properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view src/main.jsx import Chart from 'chart.js/auto'; function renderChart(canvas) { new Chart(canvas, { type: 'bar', data: { labels: ['S', 'M', 'T', 'W', 'T', 'F'], datasets: [ { label: '# of Votes', data: [12, 19, 3, 5, 2, 3], borderWidth: 1, }, ], }, options: { plugins: { legend: { display: false, }, }, scales: { y: { beginAtZero: true, }, }, }, }); } function render(element) { const canvas = document.createElement('canvas'); element.appendChild(canvas); renderChart(canvas); } context.set('ui', render);

searchDocs.title: datatype
searchDocs.content: datatype The datatype Property field provides a hint to Openexus and users as to what kind of thing a Property can hold. This in turn steers what a Property can connect to and interact with. datatypes are useful indicators on how properties can communicate with other properties. Here's just a small example smattering of datatype usage... properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view slot: datatype: 'web-view[]' some_datatype_I_have: datatype: text some_action: datatype: action properties: - key: id datatype: text some_trigger: datatype: trigger your_secret: datatype: secret Types​ Primitive datatypes​ Standard primitive datatypes are simple, fundamental structures. text - Holds text like "Openexus is great!". This is sometimes called a "string" in other programming languages and systems. boolean - A type that can be either true or false, nothing else. number - Holds a number value, be it a whole numer or a real number. Dates​ Support for working with Dates and Times. Please also see js-date - Holds the date in a JavaScript Date() object. Compound datatypes​ Compound types are types that are a compond of other types. Examples include arrays, object, json, maps, dictionaries, and lists. [_type_] - Array of a certain type (remember to replace _type_ with one of the primitives) For example: [boolean] which can hold values like: [ true , false , true ] json - Holds a JavaScript object For example: json => { a : 1, b : 2 }. json-text - Holds a JavaScript object in string format => "{a:1,b:2}". option - Holds a list of options you specify. You have to list the options with the datatype as well. For example: position: datatype: type: option options: - top - bottom UI & Slot datatypes​ Specific to the rendering of a Module, these types indicates that the Property will have a function that will return HTML. html - Holds the rendered output of a Module. This means when used, the HTML of the Module will be returned for that Module. 'web-view[]' - Holds a slot input into a Module, which is an array of html. Usually used to join up other html types together into a layout. Trigger datatype​ trigger - A trigger datatype is a special type that is used to notify of some event on a Module. When an event is fired or emitted from the Module, any connection to the associated trigger will be notified. For example, a button Module may have a on_click property with datatype: trigger. trigger properties can only connect to action properties. Action datatype​ action - An action datatype is a special type that is used to execute or run some behavior of the Module. When an action receives notification from a trigger, the associated behavior is executed. For example, on_click (trigger) can be connected to a send_email (action). It may be helpful to think of an action as a function or block of code that can execute when a trigger connected to it has an event. action properties can only connect to trigger properties. Any datatype​ The any datatype means that a Property can accept connections from any other datatype. Largely, one should avoid using any as a datatype as it will make connections harder to use. Extended datatypes​ Extended datatypes are datatypes which derive themselves from a more common parent type, such as the types above. As such, they can connect to properties with the parent type in addition to those of the same type. For example, a email type can connect to another email type or to it's parent type of text. Note: Some Extended datatypes may be validated to make sure they conform to their specific type needs and setting a value on these properties may throw errors if they fail validation. For example, an email type is validated to ensure that it meets Email Address formatting. Extends text​ The following types all extend the text datatype and thus can connect to properties of the same type or properties of type text. For example, a email type can connect to another email type or to it's parent type of text. Extends text (Identity)​ email - Holds an email in plain text. Validated to check if it is in email format (has an @ sign). name - Holds a person's full name in plain text. first-name - Holds a person's first name in plain text. last-name - Holds a person's last name in plain text. username - Holds a username in plain text. password - Holds a password in plain text. Extends text (Secrets)​ secret - Holds a reference to a secret value that cannot be displayed, only used. Usually for API keys or holding sensitive passwords. A secret type is intentionally obscured from users and developers to protect their contents and avoid exposing this information. The secret is only fetched when it is needed in a module. For more information about Secrets, please read the Using Secrets section. Extends text (Currency)​ currency - Holds a number and a currency. currency-alpha - Holds the currency in plain text as a 3 letter currency code (ISO 4217). For example: USD, EUR, JPY cc-number - Holds a Credit Card number in plain text. Validated to check that the value matches known Credit Card Number standards. Same as credit-card-number below. credit-card-number - Holds a Credit Card number in plain text. Validated to check that the value matches known Credit Card Number standards. Same as cc-number above. Extends text (Technical)​ url - Holds a URL in plain text. Validated to check if it is in URL format (starts with http:// or https://). uuid - Holds a Universally Unique Identifier in plain text. Validated to check if it is in uuid format (36 alphanumeric with dashes). ip - Holds an Internet Protocol address in plain text. This may be either an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Validated to check if it is in an IPv4 or IPv6 address format. ipv4 - Holds an Internet Protocol address in plain text. This must be an IPv4 address. Validated to check if it is in an IPv4 address format. ipv6 - Holds an Internet Protocol address in plain text. This must be an IPv6 address. Validated to check if it is in an IPv6 address format. sql-statement - Holds an sql statement in plain text. jmes-path - Holds a jmes-path in plain text. css-stylesheet - Holds a css-stylesheet in plain text. css-unit - Holds a css-unit in plain text. For example: 12px, 1rem, 2em, etc Extends text (Colors)​ css-color - Holds a css color in plain text. These may be of any supported CSS color expression form. Please see MDN <color> value documenation for more details. color-css - Holds a password in plain text. These may be of any supported CSS color expression form. Please see MDN <color> value documenation for more details. color-hex - Holds a color represented as a hexadecimal string. color-rgb - Holds an color represented as a RGB string of three decimal octets. Extends text (Location)​ location - Holds a latitude and a longitude pair. In the format of ISO 6709 (/ is terminating, no comma). For example: "+48.8577+002.295/" country - Holds a country name in full. For example: "United States of America" country-alpha-2 - Holds a two letter country code in plain text. For example: US, CN, IN country-alpha-3 - Holds a two letter country code. For example: USA, CHN, IND timezone - Holds the timezone specified in a string. Extends text (Date and Time)​ datetime - Holds the Date and Time in plain text. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (UTC). date - Holds a Date in plain text. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-MM-DD. time - Holds a Time in plain text. In the format of ISO 8601: hh:mm:ss. timezone - Holds the timezone specified in a string. In the format of ISO-8601 Time Zone. For example: +04:00 year-week - Holds a date in plain text with the year and week. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-Wxx. For example: 2024-W18 year-week-day - Holds a date in plain text with the year, week and day. ISO 8601: YYYY-W1xx-x. For example: 2024-W18-4 year-ordinal-date - Holds a date in plain text with the year, ordinal and day. ISO 8601: YYYY-ddd. For example: 2024-123 year-month - Holds a date in plain text with the year and month. In the format of ISO 8601: YYYY-MM. Extends number​ The following types all extend the number datatype and thus can connect to properties of the same type or properties of type number. Extends number (Currency)​ currency-numeric - Holds the currency as a 3 digit number currency code (ISO 4217). For example: 840, 978, 392 Extends number (Location)​ country-code-numeric - Holds a number referring to a country. E.g 840, 156, 356 zipcode-us - Holds a US zipcode in as a number. For example: 94043 Extends number (Date and Time)​ datetime-epoch - Holds the datetime (Unix Epoch/POSIX time) in plain text as a number. For example: 1618921342 Other datatypes​ The following additional datatypes are also supported. pointer-event - Holds the pointer event of a mouse/touch event. data - Holds general data from an API response. image - Holds an image in the form of a blob string. file - Holds a file in the form of a blob or URL reference. Default Type​ If no datatype is specified for a Property, the default type of any is used. As we mention above, it is undesirable to use the any type, so please avoid not providing a datatype for properties. Datatypes & Connections​ Datatypes provide a useful hint as to how Modules can communicate with each other, similar to typing in a programming language. Some common rules are: any can always connect with any other Property, irregardless of datatype.trigger datatypes can only be connected with action datatypes. Platforms that implement the spec can decide how to treat connections with different datatypes. On openexus, when different datatypes are connected (For example: number to text), we will provide a warning to the user and also try our best to cast the datatypes accordingly. datatype Coercion​ When you connect two properties together of differing datatypes, Openexus will attempt to coerce one datatype into another as appropriate. searchDocs.title: Views
searchDocs.content: Views Some Modules may want to render output to the screen. In order to do this, the Module must expose a Property to render this content. We call these Properties "View properties". NOTE: Not all Modules will have a View Property. Only Modules that have a visual component to them should have a View Property. If a Module does not have a visual component to it, it does not need to have a View Property. Creating View Properties​ To create a View Property, create a Property in your Property declaration that has a datatype of html. This indicates to Openexus that the output of this property is a render function or render content. A render function is a function which takes a parent element and produces a rendered result. This result may be to either mutate the parent element, or to produce a block of HTML content to insert. Here's an example of creating a View Property: properties.yaml view: datatype: web-view NOTE: A View Property does not have to use the property key view. Other keys can be used. However, using view is a standard approach in Openexus and encouraged. Rendering​ A render function is a JavaScript/TypeScript function that gets called when any part of the Instance changes. These changes trigger rendering and the render function gets called to produce the new output. The render function is called with the following signature: (parentElement: HTMLElement) => string The parentElement argument is a reference to the element in which the result of the render function will be rendered. For some frameworks this is reqviewred, for others it is not. The returned string from the render function is any valid HTML content including HTML Tags. This content is directly inserted into the parentElement to produce the final view of the module instance. Setting a View Property​ A View Property is just a Property that takes as a value the render function. It is critical to make sure to set your View Property to the function being used to render, as shown here in this code: properties.yaml view: datatype: web-view src/main.js function render() { return `<p>Hello there!</p>`; } context.set('view', render) In the above, the function named render is set as the value of the view Property. Working with Frameworks​ Each framework will have its own approach to rendering. These might include creating elements or using JSX/TSX. Because each framework is different, they may have slight differences how the render function works. Please consult our extensive Framework documentation to learn more details. Example​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid Simple counter button example without using any external libraries. manifest.yaml name: Counter (JavaScript) description: An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. categories: starter/javascript,starter/vanilla keywords: starter,javascript,vanilla,counter icon: logos:javascript compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow properties.yaml view: datatype: web-view count: datatype: number description: The number of times the button has been clicked since this application was started. This represents using a simple Property in the Openexus system. default: 1 src/main.js /** * An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple * button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. */ let button; // Define a render function to return our HTMLElement to display. function render() { // Create the element. button = document.createElement('button'); // Populate the element. button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; // Openexus components use tailwind by default, but you can define CSS // classes and styles in your preferred manner. button.classList.add('bg-blue-500', 'hover:bg-blue-700', 'text-white', 'py-2', 'px-4', 'rounded'); // For our button we want to mutate our count state when it is clicked. button.addEventListener('click', (value) => { context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); }); return button; } // Register to be notified when ((count)) changes. context.subscribe('count', (value) => { if (button) button.innerHTML = `Count is ${value}`; }); // Set our render function to the ((ui)) property for rendering. context.set('ui', context.render(render));

searchDocs.title: Property Injection
searchDocs.content: Property Injection A small set of properties are injected into all (or most) instances automatically. All Instances​ All Instances have the following Properties injected automatically. name - The name of this instance. Populated by default from the name field of the Manifest.description - A description of this instance. Populated by default from the description field of the Manifest.icon - An icon for this instance. Populated by default from the icon field of the Manifest. View Instances​ Instances that have a view property will also have the following properties automatically injected into them: css - Any additional CSS to apply to the view provided. This field takes any valid CSS content as described here: MDN Cascading Style Sheet Example​

searchDocs.title: Rendering
searchDocs.content: Rendering For modules that produce visual output the ability to render that output is key. Whether a module uses Vanilla JS/TS, or Vue, or Svelte, or Solid, or React, rendering output into the HTML DOM Tree is necessary. For those cases, the Openexus SDK provides the context.render() function. context.render(<render-function>); context.render() takes as its sole argument a function that returns an HTMLElement object. This object is then appended to the DOM Tree as the output for the module. Here we show a simple usage of context.render(), in this case using vanilla JS/TS. // Define a render function to return our HTMLElement to display. function render() { // Create the element. button = document.createElement('button'); // Populate the element. button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; // Classes and styles in your preferred manner. button.classList.add('bg-blue-500', 'hover:bg-blue-700', 'text-white', 'py-2', 'px-4', 'rounded'); return button; } // Set our render function to the ((ui)) property for rendering. context.set('ui', context.render(render)); Examples​ VanillaReactVueSvelteSolid manifest.yaml name: Counter (JavaScript) description: An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. categories: starter/javascript,starter/vanilla keywords: starter,javascript,vanilla,counter icon: logos:javascript compiler: vanilla environment: browser sandbox: browser.shadow properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view count: datatype: number description: The number of times the button has been clicked since this application was started. This represents using a simple Property in the Openexus system. default: 1 src/main.js /** * An example using JavaScript and no framework to render a simple * button that displays the number of times the button is clicked. */ let button; // Define a render function to return our HTMLElement to display. function render() { // Create the element. button = document.createElement('button'); // Populate the element. button.innerHTML = `Count is ${context.get('count')}`; // Openexus components use tailwind by default, but you can define CSS // classes and styles in your preferred manner. button.classList.add('bg-blue-500', 'hover:bg-blue-700', 'text-white', 'py-2', 'px-4', 'rounded'); // For our button we want to mutate our count state when it is clicked. button.addEventListener('click', (value) => { context.set('count', context.get('count') + 1); }); return button; } // Register to be notified when ((count)) changes. context.subscribe('count', (value) => { if (button) button.innerHTML = `Count is ${value}`; }); // Set our render function to the ((ui)) property for rendering. context.set('ui', context.render(render));

searchDocs.title: Properties Declaration
searchDocs.content: Properties Declaration The Properties declaration describes a Module's data points, the input and output of a Module. When a Module receives input from another Module it comes across one of these properties. When a Module produces output of any type, it sends that output by way of one of these properties. Properties consist of a property key and zero or more optional configuration details. properties.yaml value: description: Provide a number, and get back the double value in ((double)). datatype: number default: 1 order: 20 double: description: The doubled value. order: 10 readonly: true Property Keys​ Each Property needs to have a unique key. This is the key that will be used for referencing this Property and performing value lookups against it. Requirements for a key are as follows: Keys are case sensitive.A key must start with alpha character of the form [A-Z] or [a-z].A key may have an alpha character of the form [A-Z] or [a-z].A key may have a numeric character of the form [0-9], but it may not be the first character.A key may have an underscore character, but it may not be the first character. Once a Module is published and in-use by others, changing the key may affect existing connections. Property datatype​ A Property datatype is an additional configuration point for a Property. The datatype of a Property describes what type of values of data that Property can hold. This is used when two Modules are connected together. Connections are only possible if they datatype of the two Properties being connected are aligned. If a property is missing a datatype, the default datatype is applied and used. The datatype of a property is specified by the datatype field of the property configuration. Possible datatypes are described in the datatype property documentation. One special datatype to be aware of is the secret datatype. To read more about it visit the section on Using Secrets. It is strongly recommended that a datatype be included for each Property. Do not rely on the default datatype. It is very loose and will not combine with other types well. Property Fields​ datatype: The type of data this field holds. Possible values are described in the datatype property documentation.default: the default value of the property field.description: A short, human readable description of the property field.direction: The directionality of the property field. Possible values are described in the direction property documenation.documentation: Longer form documentation for the property field, if needed. group: A logical grouping for propeties. A property that is given a group will be visually grouped together with properties of the same group when visually displayed. If no group is given, the properties are not grouped. More details can be found in the group property documenation.hidden: If true this property is hidden and not shown when the Module is displayed visually.name: The name or label of this property. Has a maximum of 256 characters. If a name is not provided, Openexus will use the key and attempt to format it nicely. This may not always be quite correct, so feel free to use the name field to override that behavior.order: The importance of the property; a higher number indicates more importance. More details can be found in the order property documenation. required: If true this property is required to have a value. value: The value of the property field. This differs from the default in that the default is used ONLY IF the value is not set. Examples​ Some examples of Property Declarations. properties.yaml ui: datatype: web-view data: purpose: Incoming data to display on a table. Commonly connected to the [result] property of api modules so that we can show data. Array of objects are required to show in a table. If an object instead of an array is provided instead, this module can best guess the array to display in the table. If the guess is incorrect, [data_query] property can be used to transform the data to an array. datatype: json order: 10 data_query: description: Transform the data using JMESPath (https://jmespath.org). purpose: "Transform the data using JMESPath (https://jmespath.org). You can use common dot notion to transverse the data object. For example, given an object { list: [1,2,3] }, setting [data_query] as '.list' will return just the array [1,2,3]. If the intention is to selective only show some columns, use the [columns] property, do not need to use the [data_query] property." datatype: json order: 10 table_columns: name: Columns description: Columns to show. purpose: Define the columns to show in the table. Update this property if we want to selectively only show some columns from the given data. If not provided, all columns would be shown. Update this property with a comma seperated string. For example, "id,name,rating" will only show the id, name, and rating keys from the given object. datatype: text order: 10 selected_row: description: Data for the selected row. purpose: Get the data for the selected row. This can be useful to connect the selected data to show additional details. datatype: any selected_row_index: description: Selected row index. datatype: number properties.yaml result: purpose: Result of the NASA Earth Imagery which returns a satelite image of a specified point and dimension on earth. order: 10 datatype: image api_key: datatype: text default: niceTry hidden: true lat: description: Latitude of the satelite image to get datatype: text required: true lon: description: Longitude of the satelite image to get datatype: text required: true dim: description: Dimension of the image in degrees datatype: text default: 0.025 date: description: Date to fetch in YYYY-MM-DD datatype: text required: true default: "2024-05-01"
